opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one of the trade-offs we spent a lot of time agonizing over with Aya. There's this phenomenon people call the "curse of multilinguality," which is essentially that when you have a fixed capacity model and you keep adding languages, at some point the performance per language starts to degrade. Every language is competing for the same parameters. So there's a real tension: you want breadth, because the whole point is to serve people who've historically been left out, but you don't want to spread the model so thin that it's mediocre at everything.

So the way I think about it is, model size buys you capacity, and capacity is what lets you cover more languages without that interference really biting. If you're going to go very wide, say a hundred-plus languages, you generally need a bigger base to absorb that. But bigger isn't free. It's more expensive to serve, and a lot of the communities we care about are exactly the ones that don't have access to huge compute. So deploying a massive model can undercut the very goal of accessibility.

What we've found is that it's less a single dial and more about being deliberate. One, what the base model already saw in pretraining matters enormously. If the base was trained mostly on English, you're fighting the tokenizer and the representations the whole way, and fine-tuning can only recover so much. So I'd often rather pick a somewhat smaller base that was genuinely multilingual from the start than a larger one that's English-dominant. Two, there's a lot you can do in the data mix, things like how you weight and sample across languages, using translated and synthetic data carefully, and techniques like merging, that let you push the frontier of that trade-off rather than just accepting it.

And then, you know, I think we also learned that sometimes it's worth being more focused. With Aya 23, for instance, we deliberately covered fewer languages than the earlier, very broad model, so we could allocate more capacity to each and get much stronger performance. The broad model is really valuable for coverage and for research, and the focused one gives you depth. I don't think there's one right answer. It depends on who you're building for and what the deployment constraints look like. But I'd encourage people to stop treating it as just "make it bigger" and actually think about where capacity is going.

r001.rationale: It says greater capacity lets a model cover more languages with less interference, and that very broad coverage generally needs a bigger base.

r002.rationale: It explains that with fixed capacity, adding languages makes them compete for parameters and can degrade performance per language.

r003.rationale: It favors a somewhat smaller base that was multilingual from pretraining, but does not suggest that a larger base pretrained on fewer languages can be a valuable foundation for adding a broader language set during fine-tuning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is a really interesting question, and I think it's one that we've thought about a lot, because when we started the Aya project, the whole premise was that we wanted to cover a lot of languages. We ended up at 101 languages, and that was a deliberate choice, right? Because if you look at the landscape of what's available, most pretrained models are either English-dominant or they cover maybe a handful of high-resource languages. And so we had to think about what's the trade-off there.

I think the honest answer is that it's not a clean trade-off where more languages is always better or bigger is always better. What we've observed, and this is consistent with a lot of the literature on what people call the curse of multilinguality, is that when you have a fixed capacity, a fixed number of parameters, and you keep adding languages, at some point you start to see degradation. The languages start competing for the same representational space, and the per-language performance drops. So there's a real cost to breadth.

But the way I think about it is that model size is somewhat of a lever you can use to relieve that pressure. A larger model gives you more room, so you can afford to cover more languages before you hit that saturation point. So those two decisions are coupled. You can't really choose the number of languages independently of the size.

In practice, though, I'd say the question of which languages are covered in pretraining matters more to me than the raw size. Because what we see is that if a language wasn't seen during pretraining, or was seen very minimally, fine-tuning on it afterwards gets you some of the way, but you're really fighting against the base model. The tokenizer is a big part of this too. If the tokenizer wasn't built with that language in mind, you end up with these really fragmented token sequences, and the model is just working much harder for every word. So I'd rather start from a base that has genuine coverage of the languages I care about, even if it's a bit smaller, than start from a larger model that has basically only seen English and a few European languages.

The other thing I'd add is that for a lot of the languages we care about, the data is the real constraint, not the model. You can have a huge model, but if you have very little high-quality data in Kinyarwanda or in Sinhala, that size isn't buying you much for those languages. So part of our effort with Aya was actually on the data side, building the instruction datasets, working with communities, because that's what ultimately determines whether the coverage is meaningful or just nominal. A lot of models claim to support a language, and the question is really what level of quality is behind that claim.

So if I were to summarize, I'd say I weigh coverage and quality of coverage first, then think about size as the thing that lets you scale that coverage without sacrificing per-language performance. And I'd always be a bit skeptical of a very large number of languages in a small model, because that's usually where you see the biggest gap between what's advertised and what actually works.

r001.rationale: The response says that adding languages at fixed capacity causes degradation and that a larger model provides more room to cover more languages.

r002.rationale: It states that languages compete for representational space at fixed capacity, causing per-language performance to drop.

r003.rationale: The response instead favors a smaller base with genuine pretraining coverage of the target languages, and says fine-tuning languages absent from pretraining is limited. It does not endorse a larger, narrower-pretrained base as valuable for broadening language coverage through fine-tuning.

astra-6.text:
I’d be careful about treating either model size or the number of languages as a sufficient measure on its own. A model can claim to cover a hundred languages, but that doesn’t tell you whether it’s useful in the particular languages you care about. You want to understand how its capacity and its training data are distributed across those languages.

There’s a real trade-off: sharing a model across languages can enable transfer, which is especially valuable when data is scarce. But with a fixed amount of capacity, adding languages can also introduce competition. Making the model larger may help, but it doesn’t automatically fix an imbalance in the data.

So I’d start with the languages and tasks you need to support, evaluate performance in each of them, and then weigh that against the cost of serving the model. I’d be particularly wary of averages that hide poor performance in lower-resource languages. The question is less, ‘How many languages does this model cover?’ and more, ‘How well does it serve the people we’re building it for?’

r001.rationale: The response says that adding languages can create competition at fixed capacity and that a larger model may help. It does not state that representing more languages requires greater capacity.

r002.rationale: The response mentions competition when adding languages, but does not clearly state that those languages can come at the expense of performance in other languages.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that a model pretrained on fewer languages could serve as a base for adding languages during fine-tuning.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking which languages you actually need to serve and how well they’re represented in pretraining. A model that lists a hundred languages doesn’t necessarily perform well across all of them. That headline number can hide enormous differences in the amount and quality of data available for each language.

There is a capacity trade-off: when you hold model size fixed and add languages, you’re asking the same parameters to support more tasks. Sharing can help, particularly between related languages, but it can also create interference. Increasing model size can ease that pressure, though it doesn’t automatically solve poor data coverage.

So I wouldn’t choose on parameter count or language count alone. I’d evaluate the candidate bases on the languages and tasks that matter, look at performance language by language, and weigh that against the cost of deploying them. A smaller model with strong coverage of your target languages may be a better starting point than a much larger model with broad but uneven coverage.

r001.rationale: It explains that adding languages puts more demands on fixed parameters and that increasing model size can ease that capacity pressure.

r002.rationale: It mentions possible interference, but does not clearly state that adding languages can reduce performance for other languages when capacity is insufficient.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest using a larger model pretrained on fewer languages and broadening language coverage during fine-tuning.
